newsitem.title: Afghanistan: Hopes of Afghan ceasefire fade.
newsitem.headline: Hopes of Afghan ceasefire fade.

text.p: Ceasefire talks between warring Afghan factions appear to be nearing collapse, making a new push on Kabul by anti-Taleban forces increasingly likely, Afghan watchers said on Thursday.
"Our understanding is that their positions are still far apart and the gap appears unbridgeable," said a veteran Afghan watcher.
"It looks like it's a question of when rather than whether they collapse and if they do then a significant offensive down the plain to Kabul seems inevitable," he said.
There has been heavy fighting north of Kabul during days of ceasefire talks brokered by Pakistani Interior Minister Naseerullah Babar and U.N. Special Envoy Norbert Holl.

Holl saw northern Uzbek chief Abdul Rashid Dostum in his stronghold of Mazar-i-Sharif on Wednesday and was due to fly to Kandahar, headquarters of the purist Taleban movement, on Thursday for further talks.

He appeared to have only slim hopes of pulling off a ceasefire, with Dostum and his ally, former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood, demanding the demilitarisation of Kabul. The Taleban, whose fighters captured Kabul on September 27, have rejected the condition as unacceptable.
"Success is far from being guaranteed," Holl said after talking to Dostum.
"I suspect that's diplomatic language for there's little hope," said the Afghan watcher.

Another Afghan watcher with a military background said all the signs were that a major battle was likely on the plain north of Kabul, where Dostum sent tanks, artillery and men to join Masood's front line last week.
"The Taleban are beginning for the first time to put in some defence in depth just outside the Kabul valley and that's a sign they are expecting something," he said.
The militia, which controls three-quarters of Afghanistan, installed three artillery pieces alongside several tanks and rocket launchers on Wednesday about six km (four miles) outside the valley.

On Thursday, Masood's forces lobbed mortar rounds into Taleban positions in the long village of Hussein Kot, of which both sides control part, but fighters said there had been no change in the front line.
Nor was there any immediate sign of a major offensive. A steady stream of refugees fled the area.

"But the fact is that if Masood and Dostum move together, they probably have the strength to punch through the Taleban lines on both sides of the plain and drive all the way to Kabul," said the analyst with a military background.

Whether Dostum has sent his ground forces into action is not clear, and the Taleban say there is no evidence that he has. If he did, they say, he would be regarded as an enemy rather than someone they can do business with.
"It seems to me that the only question left is whether Masood and Dostum will actually try to take the city," the analyst said.

He and others said that if Masood did try to take Kabul he would create another bloodbath in a city marked by ruins from previous factional battles and that he would probably not want to squander popular support by doing so.
